name: linkinator
description: Broken-link checker and site crawler with CLI + API; scans remote sites, local HTML and Markdown, validates any element containing a link, configurable skip regexes; standalone binaries and a Docker image (ghcr.io/justinbeckwith/linkinator).
verdict: Yes — wire it into CI in under a minute. Not an SEO auditor, only a link checker; use it alongside, not instead of, a crawler.

name: LibreCrawl
description: Multi-tenant web app (Python/Flask + MongoDB) that crawls a site and reports pages, links, SEO elements and performance; explicitly positioned as a free Screaming Frog/DeepCrawl/Sitebulb replacement with a plugin workshop.
verdict: Yes if you want a hosted, multi-seat crawler UI. Single maintainer, sponsorship-funded, no paid tier — treat as a solo-maintainer dependency, not a vendor.

name: SiteOne Crawler
description: Rust rewrite of a cross-platform crawler/analyzer: single static binary (Win/macOS/Linux, x64+arm64), HTML/JSON/text reports with 0-10 quality scoring, sitemap generation, offline site clones, whole-site Markdown export, --ci quality gate (exit code 10) and post-deploy cache warming.
verdict: Yes — best-in-class for CI integration and for shipping your own content to LLMs as Markdown. The single most useful open alternative to Screaming Frog today.

name: SEOnaut
description: Go + MySQL open-source SEO audit tool: full site scan, issues bucketed critical/high/low (broken links, redirect loops, missing/duplicate meta, heading order), ECharts dashboard, Docker Compose deploy.
verdict: Yes, but only for a Go/MySQL shop. Thin feature set versus LibreCrawl/siteone-crawler; live at seonaut.org.

name: crawlseo
description: Self-hosted dashboard combining Google Search Console, a site crawler (2,000 pages/crawl default), Core Web Vitals, index status, BYOK keyword research and backlinks, plus a strictly read-only MCP server; Docker Compose on your own PostgreSQL.
verdict: Yes, if you want one small app instead of six. BYOK (DataForSEO) for keywords/backlinks, Google Autocomplete as the free fallback.

name: open-seo-crawler
description: Self-hosted Python crawler/audit that also checks whether AI crawlers can reach the site; ships as a web app with an API.
verdict: Only if AI-crawler reachability is the specific gap you have. Small project (81 stars), verify it still runs before adopting.

name: DeepCrawl
description: Cloud crawler with large-scale scheduling, JavaScript rendering and bot-management-aware crawling; subscription per account.
verdict: Skip for a personal site. Overkill until you are crawling many domains on a schedule.

name: Screaming Frog SEO Spider
description: Desktop crawler, the de-facto technical SEO standard. Free tier 500 URLs; paid licence 1-4 seats GBP 199 per licence per year (renewal required), unlimited URLs, JS rendering, custom extraction, scheduling, segmentation, GSC/GA/PageSpeed integrations, Looker Studio crawl reports.
verdict: Buy one seat at GBP 199 if a client ever needs a crawl you cannot do in open source. For your own site, siteone-crawler covers 80% of it for free.

name: Sitebulb
description: Browser-based SaaS crawler with a spreadsheet UI, JavaScript rendering, site health, link and performance analysis; no per-URL pricing, subscription per user.
verdict: Only if you want zero-install CSV-style audits for non-technical stakeholders. Otherwise LibreCrawl + siteone-crawler.

name: Lighthouse
description: The audit engine behind PageSpeed Insights: performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, and — since v13.2 (audit merged 2026-04-20) — an 'agentic browsing' category that includes an llms.txt audit (core/audits/agentic/llms-txt.js) checking the file is fetchable, has an H1, is long enough and contains links.
verdict: Yes. It is the reference implementation of the metrics that matter and now also the only mainstream lms.txt linter.

name: web-vitals
description: The tiny front-end library that reports LCP, INP, CLS and FCP from real users via the PerformanceObserver API — the standard way to collect your own field data.
verdict: Yes — 4 KB, no dependencies, and the only way to get true INP/LCP field numbers for your own pages.

name: Lighthouse CI
description: Runs Lighthouse on every commit, stores and diffs the results, asserts configurable budgets so a perf or SEO regression fails the build.
verdict: Yes — the highest-leverage CI piece in this entire list. Wire it to your static site on day one.

name: sitespeed.io
description: Web performance testing and monitoring at scale: browser-based runs, WebPageTest-like budgets, CI integration, long-term trend storage and a Grafana/InfluxDB path.
verdict: Yes for continuous field-style monitoring across many URLs. Heavier setup than lighthouse-ci for a single small site.

name: web-quality-skills
description: Agent Skills that turn Lighthouse + Chrome DevTools MCP + Core Web Vitals + WCAG 2.2 into measurement-first instructions for agents: live audits, performance traces, CrUX field context, LCP/INP/CLS fix patterns.
verdict: Yes if you already run agents over your site. It teaches the agent to measure before changing anything — the discipline most AI SEO tools lack.

name: SearXNG
description: AGPL-3.0 metasearch engine that aggregates many search services without tracking users; self-hosted, JSON API enabled.
verdict: Yes as a privacy-preserving research/SERP front end for agents. Not a substitute for a commercial SERP API for rank tracking.

name: SerpBear
description: Open-source rank tracker: unlimited domains and keywords, scheduled SERP checks, change notifications by email, a built-in API and a Docker image on Docker Hub.
verdict: Yes — the default self-hosted rank tracker. Needs a SERP provider key underneath; it is the dashboard, not the data.

name: search-console-mcp
description: MCP server for Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools: exposes search and analytics data to Claude/Cursor as a data layer rather than a set of instructions.
verdict: Yes if you want an agent querying GSC directly. Pairs naturally with the agent-skills layer.

name: SerpScrap
description: Python library/CLI that retrieves structured search results for SEO, research and automation.
verdict: Only if you need raw SERP HTML without a paid API. Check its proxy/ToS posture before running it at volume.

name: google-browser-scraper
description: Self-hosted Google SERP scraper driving a real Chrome browser via CDP, so results are not the stripped-down JSON a plain HTTP client sees.
verdict: Useful escape hatch when a SERP API is too coarse. Fragile and ToS-sensitive; treat as a diagnostic, not a pipeline.

name: SearchMirror
description: Self-hosted Google rank tracker plus AI-visibility monitor: positions by country/language/device, competitor comparison, Geo Citations (AI brand-mention checks using your own provider keys), content planner. Explicitly pre-1.0 with a legacy Django 3.2 / MongoDB 4.4 stack.
verdict: Not yet. The pre-1.0 warning and Django 3.2 runtime are real blockers — watch it, do not deploy it.

name: SEO Playground
description: Self-hosted SEO and Local SEO dashboard on the DataForSEO API: rankings, LLM prompt tracking, geo-grid visibility scans (square/diamond/circle, rotated, mileage or km), review velocity vs local competitors, broken backlink detection, PDF/Excel reports.
verdict: Yes for local SEO — the geo-grid and review-velocity features are things no open-source rank tracker has. Disclosed DataForSEO affiliate link; budget accordingly.

name: OpenGSC
description: Self-hosted Google Search Console dashboard on your own VPS: rank tracking, keyword research, AI-visibility audits, an AI SEO content suite and a private indexing network; one-line installer, Next.js 16 + TypeScript, v1.13.1.
verdict: Yes if you want a private GSC console and do not want to hand Google credentials to a third-party SaaS. Verify the private indexer before pointing it at production.

name: SerpTrail
description: Self-hosted Ruby on Rails + SQLite rank tracker: multi-site, multi-keyword, multi-location, scheduled checks, historical SERP storage, AI-Overview citation tracking, OpenAI chat assistant over history, and a SerpApi credit estimator.
verdict: Yes if you want AI-Overview citation tracking with historical SERP retention and you are comfortable with Rails. Small project (50 stars) — read the code before trusting it with a client domain.

name: DataForSEO
description: Pay-as-you-go API family: SERP API, Keyword Data, Backlinks, Domain Analytics, On-Page, Labs (AI-optimization endpoints included), Business Data. Minimum first payment $50.
verdict: Yes for keyword volume, backlinks and on-page at scale without a $130+/mo subscription — but budget per-request, not per-seat.

name: SerpApi
description: SERP API with per-engine endpoints including Google AI Overview, Google AI Mode, Google Jobs, Google News, Bing Copilot, Duck AI and Perplexity. Free 250 searches/month; Starter $25/mo (1,000 searches), Developer $75/mo (5,000), Production $150/mo (15,000), Big Data $275/mo (30,000); enterprise custom.
verdict: Buy the $25 starter while you build. It is the single most useful paid API here: it is the only mainstream one with a first-class Google AI Overview endpoint.

name: gtm-engineer-skills
description: Claude Code skills for AEO/GEO GTM work: research-brand, research-keywords, geo-content-research, geo-content-planning, write-seo-geo-content, create-geo-charts, audit-content, build-backlinks, audit-website-aeo, improve-aeo-geo — each skill emits a reviewable artifact file rather than chat prose.
verdict: Yes if you want agent-generated artifacts with a human review step. Closest thing to an end-to-end GEO content pipeline in open source.

name: geo-optimizer-skill
description: Open-source engine behind GeoReady: one command scores any site 0-100 on whether ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Google AI Overviews can crawl, understand and cite it, across nine categories, then prints the fixes. pip/uvx install, no API key, no account.
verdict: Yes — the cheapest way to get a repeatable GEO score for a URL. Audit only: it does not track over time.

name: Elmo
description: Self-hosted open-source AEO/GEO platform: tracks how ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews mention, cite and describe your brand — visibility score, share of voice, sentiment, position, citation domains/URLs, and the query fan-out the engines ran. Positions itself as the free alternative to Profound/Peec/Otterly; hosted cloud from $29/mo.
verdict: Yes — the most complete open AI-visibility tracker I verified. Use it if you can supply your own model API keys.

name: GEORank
description: Python GEO workbench: site diagnosis (schema, page structure, meta, readability, citation signals), structured AI Q&A, 30/60/90-day action plans, keyword/question expansion, JSON-LD + llms.txt + title generation, and an admin module for private deployment with your own model API keys.
verdict: Yes, and it is the only open tool I verified that actually generates llms.txt and JSON-LD from a diagnosis. UI and docs are Chinese-first; English README exists.

name: GetCito
description: Open-source AI Search Optimization platform: prompt/topic organization, query fan-out exploration, brand mentions, sentiment and citation tracking across answer engines, growth-task backlog with evidence, content briefs and drafts, site audits, AI referral traffic, REST API, MCP server, webhooks, Looker Studio connector.
verdict: Yes if you want an end-to-end agent-facing platform rather than a tracker. It is one of the few open tools exposing AI-visibility data over MCP.

name: GEO-Content-Optimizer-Skill
description: Three Chinese-language GEO skills for Claude Code/Codex: geo-content-optimizer (single-page audit by pulling the Google AI Overview for your title and diffing it against your copy), geo-optimizer (guided first-time GEO setup), geolook (recurring GEO tracking workbench).
verdict: Useful idea, weak fit: the single-page diff-against-AI-Overview pattern is worth copying; the tooling and docs are Chinese-first.

name: Ansvisor
description: Open-source agentic AI Search Execution Platform: prompt monitoring, brand mentions, sentiment, citations, competitors, AI traffic and source analysis across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, AI Mode, Gemini, Claude and Grok; an Action Center and a Content Agent that drafts fixes for human approval; REST, MCP and Looker Studio connectors.
verdict: Promising but early (234 stars, ~1 week of commit cadence at fetch time). The agent-drafts-fix-and-you-approve loop is the right shape; verify the deployment path before betting on it.

name: E-GEO (eGEOagents)
description: Open-source CLI plus Claude Code skills for GEO/AEO, built on published GEO research (arXiv 2511.20867): scores a Markdown page against generative-engine preferences, generates optimizations and citation-ready structure, includes a mock mode so it runs without an API key.
verdict: Yes for content-level work on your own Markdown. The paper-backed scoring is the differentiator; the surface is still young.

name: searchstack-aeo
description: PyPI CLI for AI-native founders: monitors visibility across Google, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity and Claude from one command, with GSC-backed rankings and a cost comparison table against Ahrefs/Semrush.
verdict: Yes as a terminal-first substitute for a $130+/mo suite. Verify which engines it actually calls before you report numbers to anyone.

name: sample-llm-search-citation-analysis (Bedrock)
description: AWS sample that tracks a brand's visibility in AI search with a citation-analysis tool built on Amazon Bedrock.
verdict: Yes as a reference implementation if you are already on Bedrock. 23 stars and sample-quality — copy the pattern, do not depend on the repo.

name: Ahrefs Brand Radar
description: AI visibility inside Ahrefs: a searchable AI index across seven platforms plus custom prompts. Custom Prompts from $50/mo (2,500 checks); AI Visibility Index $199/mo per platform or $699/mo for all platforms. Base Ahrefs plans: Starter $29/mo (research only), Lite $129/mo (750 keywords, 150 AI prompt checks, 100k crawl credits, API + MCP), Standard $249/mo, Advanced $449/mo, Enterprise $1,499/mo.
verdict: Only worth it if you already pay for Ahrefs - then it is the cheapest incremental AI-visibility add-on in the market.

name: Otterly.AI
description: Monitoring for ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, Perplexity and MS Copilot (Claude, AI Mode and Gemini as add-ons): Lite $29/mo (15 prompts), Standard $189/mo (100 prompts, API + MCP access, Agent Analytics), Premium $489/mo. Unlimited team members, daily tracking.
verdict: Cheapest credible managed entry at $29/mo — the one to try before committing to $95+ platforms.

name: Peec AI
description: AI search analytics: Starter $95/mo (50 prompts, 1 project, 3 models, daily), Pro $245/mo (150 prompts, 2 projects), Advanced $495/mo (350 prompts, 5 projects, multi-country, Looker Studio), Enterprise custom (up to 13 models, SSO, API). Unlimited users on every plan.
verdict: Reasonable mid-market option with unlimited seats. At $95/mo entry it loses to self-hosted Elmo unless you need the managed reports.

name: Profound
description: Enterprise AI-visibility platform: answer-engine insights, agent analytics and attribution across up to 9 engines, agents, context manager, sheets. Public pricing page shows a free Trial (50 prompts daily for 7 days, ChatGPT + Gemini + AI Overviews) and Enterprise 'custom' - no self-serve paid tier is published.
verdict: Only for enterprise budgets. At solo scale the free Elmo/self-hosted route covers the same metrics at zero licence cost.

name: SE Ranking
description: SEO+GEO suite: Core $129/mo ($103.20 annual) — 10 projects, 2k keywords, 100 prompts tracked daily, 5 domains in GEO research, 250k pages/mo audit, 25k API credits, MCP access; Growth $279/mo ($223.20 annual) with 30 projects, 5k keywords, 250 prompts, 15 GEO domains, 2M pages/mo, 100k credits.
verdict: Yes — best value in the paid tier: 100 daily AI prompts inside a full SEO suite for $103–129/mo, with MCP access.

name: Scrunch AI
description: Sitecore-owned AEO platform. Core $250/mo: 4 LLMs (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AIO, Copilot), 125 unique prompts, 5,000 responses/month, 1 country, 1 language, 5 competitors, 5 site audits/month, 5 licences. Enterprise adds 9 LLMs (incl. Claude, Gemini, Grok, AI Mode), unlimited countries, custom prompt volumes, API and MCP access.
verdict: Skip unless you are an enterprise buyer. $250/mo buys less model coverage and fewer prompts than the $29-95 tiers.

name: Semrush AI Visibility
description: SEO + AI Search plans: SEO $117.33/mo billed annually ($139 monthly) with 5 sites, 500 keywords tracked daily, AI search tracking, AI sentiment and custom prompts; Starter $165.17/mo annually ($199 monthly) adds full AI Search. Ships an MCP server and API.
verdict: Yes if you want one vendor for SEO + AI visibility + MCP. At $117/mo it is more than Elmo + a SERP API starter.

name: changedetection.io
description: Website change detection and monitoring with alerts; the classic tool for watching rendered pages (including JS-rendered AI Overviews and AI answer pages) for changes.
verdict: Yes, as a cheap competitor/answer-tracking primitive: snapshot the AI answer page you care about and diff it weekly.

name: crawler-user-agents
description: Syntactic patterns of HTTP user-agents used by bots, robots, crawlers, scrapers and spiders, kept as a pull-request-welcoming Go dataset.
verdict: Yes, as a log-parsing reference and a bot-detection library. Keep your own allowlist of AI user-agent tokens separately — this list does not distinguish training from search crawlers.

name: isbot
description: Zero-dependency, dependency-free TypeScript library that detects bots/crawlers/spiders from a user-agent string, with an extensive pattern list including AI crawlers.
verdict: Yes — drop it into your edge or log pipeline to classify AI traffic. Unlicense, so no license friction.

name: GEOInflow
description: Self-hosted web + AI crawler analytics for GEO: crawler identity, purpose, provider, request volume and verification status, repeated-crawl and directory distribution, sitemap/CSV/JSON inventory vs observed crawl coverage, HTTP status/latency/error analysis, AI referral sessions and conversions, with crawler-evidence and gap reporting. v1.2, MIT, English + Chinese docs.
verdict: Yes — the only open tool I verified that joins server-log crawler evidence to content inventory. This is the ground truth AI-visibility trackers lack.

name: schemarama
description: Google's exploration of standards-based validation for structured data, especially Schema.org, including a JSON-LD previewer.
verdict: No — archived in 2024. Use it as reference reading on how Google thinks about structured data, not as a tool.

name: @adobe/structured-data-validator
description: JS library validating structured data against both Schema.org and Google Rich Results specifications, with extensible custom type handlers; designed to pair with a web-auto-extractor.
verdict: Yes if you are validating structured data programmatically in Node. Canonical Rich-Results rule set, not a crawler.

name: ldlint
description: Fast Go CLI that validates JSON-LD against the full schema.org vocabulary — invalid properties, wrong types, schema misuse — over a directory of HTML files or a live URL, with prebuilt binaries.
verdict: Yes — cheap to run in CI over your build output, and it catches vocabulary errors the Rich Results Test misses. 1 star, but the code is short and readable.

name: Google Rich Results Test
description: Free hosted validator: paste a URL or code snippet, get Rich Results eligibility plus the exact field errors per supported type (FAQ, HowTo, Article, Product, LocalBusiness, …).
verdict: Yes — it is still the ground truth for rich-result eligibility, and it is free. Automate with ldlint, confirm here before publishing.

name: Schema Markup Validator (validator.schema.org)
description: Free official Schema.org vocabulary validator; checks types and properties against the live vocabulary and flags deprecated ones.
verdict: Yes — free and authoritative for vocabulary correctness, though it does not know Google's rich-result rules.

name: llms.txt (v2 proposal)
description: Jeremy Howard's v2 proposal for the /llms.txt file: a Markdown file at the site root giving LLMs concise background and links to detailed .md versions of pages. Documents the observed adoption (thousands of sites publishing it, Mintlify auto-generating it, Chrome Lighthouse auditing it, and OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini publishing their own).
verdict: Read it, then implement it. This is the normative spec, not a tool — but it is the reference every other llms.txt project points at.

name: mcpdoc
description: LangChain tool that exposes llms.txt content to IDEs and agents during development.
verdict: No — archived. The pattern (let the agent read your llms.txt) survives; the package does not.

name: llms-txt-hub
description: Largest public directory of AI-ready documentation and tools implementing the llms.txt standard, plus an llms.txt of its own.
verdict: Yes, as a discovery index and as a living reference of what 'llms.txt done well' looks like in practice.

name: create-llmstxt-py
description: Python example that crawls a site with Firecrawl and emits llms.txt and llms-full.txt; the successor to the now-deprecated firecrawl/llmstxt-generator.
verdict: Yes, as a generator you can run against your own site — if you already use Firecrawl. No license file and no pushes since 2025-06; treat as a starting point to fork, not a dependency.

name: marketingskills
description: Marketing Agent Skills for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf and anything speaking the Agent Skills spec: CRO, copywriting, SEO, analytics, content marketing and growth engineering, with a partner registry that is explicitly disclosed and non-steering.
verdict: Yes — the most useful general marketing skill library in open source, and the one most likely to already be in your toolchain.

name: claude-seo
description: Claude Code SEO plugin: 26 sub-skills + 19 specialist agents covering technical SEO, E-E-A-T, schema, GEO/AEO, agent readiness (Lighthouse Agentic Browsing, WebMCP, llms.txt), backlinks, local/international/e-commerce SEO, Google APIs and PDF/Excel reporting; ~1,077 tests.
verdict: Yes, if you run Claude Code. It is the most complete open SEO skill set and it already knows about llms.txt and WebMCP.

name: semrush-ai-tool
description: MIT MCP server + CLI giving agents 18 tools over the live Semrush API: keyword research, domain analytics, backlink analysis, traffic insights, competitor intelligence.
verdict: Yes if you already pay for Semrush — it is a thin, readable adapter. Requires a paid API key, so it is not a free path to Semrush-grade data.

name: dataforseo/mcp-server-typescript
description: Official DataForSEO MCP server exposing SERP, keyword-data, backlinks, on-page and Labs endpoints to MCP clients.
verdict: Yes if you are already paying DataForSEO. The most data-complete MCP adapter for paid SERP/keyword APIs.

name: seranking/seo-skills
description: Production Claude Agent Skills for the SE Ranking MCP server: content briefs, AI Search checks and reporting against SE Ranking's unified API.
verdict: Yes alongside an SE Ranking subscription. Narrowest useful case of the skill repos — but it is the official pairing.

name: dataseo-mcp
description: Free MCP server pulling backlinks, keyword difficulty, traffic estimates and keyword ideas from Ahrefs' free tools, plus AI query planning. The README explicitly flags that it automates third-party services and that you are responsible for their terms of service.
verdict: No in production. It depends on Ahrefs' free web endpoints and captcha-solving services — that is a ToS and account-risk liability, and the repo itself says so.

name: mcp-common-crawl
description: MCP server for the Common Crawl CDX index: backlink discovery across three indexes, expired/parked domain finding, competitor analysis.
verdict: Yes as a free, index-based backlink discovery source — Common Crawl is the only free source of any scale. It finds mentions, not authority. 1 star; validate output quality before relying on it.

name: santifer-irepair
description: Astro-based programmatic SEO site that generated 15,500+ unique pages from an Airtable data source — a concrete, inspectable reference implementation.
verdict: Yes as a template to read. It shows the data-model-plus-template shape that makes pSEO pages genuinely distinct rather than spun.

name: awesome-programmatic-seo
description: Curated resource for scaling organic growth through programmatic SEO: templates, tool stacks, case studies and playbooks.
verdict: Yes, as a planning reference. The honest framing it carries — pSEO needs real data per page — is the correct one under Google's scaled-content-abuse policy.

name: mcp/servers (reference servers)
description: The official Model Context Protocol reference server collection — the canonical pattern for exposing a capability to agents.
verdict: Yes as the architectural reference for anything you expose to an agent. The reference set itself is being split into per-domain collections; pull only what you use.

name: webmcp (spec)
description: The WebMCP specification: expose web app functionality as tools — JavaScript functions with natural-language descriptions and structured schemas — so in-browser agents can actuate content designed for humans. Includes a declarative HTML <form>-based API exploration; types ship as the webmcp-types npm package.
verdict: Yes, as the spec to read before building agent-accessible UI. Browser support is still in progress, so treat it as forward-looking rather than ship-blocking.

name: WebMCP (early implementation)
description: Independent, earlier WebMCP implementation — TypeScript, browser-side tool exposure for agents.
verdict: Reference implementation only. Last push was 2025-10-07; the webmachinelearning spec has moved on since.

name: webmcp-tools
description: Chrome Labs utilities and demos supporting WebMCP adoption: developer tooling, examples and adoption aids.
verdict: Yes, as the practical companion to the spec. Early but it is the reference implementation team.

name: open-seo-mcp-skills
description: MIT SEO + GEO skills for Claude with a free SEO MCP server (the Ryze connector): keyword research, rank tracking, site audits, backlinks, competitor gaps, AI visibility. Rankings come from your own Search Console and GA4 (including AI referral traffic); keyword volumes from Google Ads Keyword Planner; competitor/backlink/SERP data via DataForSEO wired into the connector, plus optional Ahrefs/Semrush connectors.
verdict: Yes, and it is the most honest architecture in this list: your own first-party data plus a clearly-labelled paid data source. The skills are MIT and forkable.

name: seo (seoskill)
description: Google Search Console MCP server and CLI for agent-native teams: your clicks, impressions and positions from GSC, visits from GA/Clicky, Bing data, Google update dates and a site crawl — as facts for the agent to reason over, not generic advice. npm package `seo`; MCP endpoint at seoskill.dev.
verdict: Yes, if you want a GSC facts layer. Note the hosted MCP endpoint: the CLI runs locally but the remote MCP service is a separate dependency.

name: SEOMonster
description: Local, user-credential-driven MCP server for SEO workflows over Google Search Console, Google Analytics and PageSpeed, running on your machine via uvx; surfaces near-ranking topics (positions 8-20 with real demand) from your own GSC and drafts the content brief. Also on PyPI.
verdict: Yes. The closest thing to 'the SEO analyst that lives in your assistant' without handing credentials to a SaaS.

name: Suganthans-GSC-MCP
description: Focused MCP server for Google Search Console: ask your assistant questions about your search data and get answers.
verdict: Yes, as the minimal GSC-only server. Redundant if you already run seo-monster or iannuttall/seo.

name: seo-audit
description: Free SEO Audit MCP server for Claude that captures and stores all the raw data needed for a complete technical audit, so the agent reasons over evidence rather than a summary.
verdict: Yes, paired with a crawler skill. Raw-evidence-first is the correct design for agent-driven audits.

name: career-ops
description: Open-source AI job search agent (Claude Code plugin, 700+ contributors): scan job boards, score each posting 1-5 against your CV, mark non-fits, tailor your CV, draft answers, and prepare interview questions. You press Submit. Local-first, MIT, 16 translated READMEs.
verdict: Yes — the strongest open job-search agent, and the honest one: it filters aggressively before it automates anything.

name: SimplifyJobs/Summer2027-Internships
description: Continuously updated list of summer 2027 SWE, data science, AI, quant, product and hardware internship postings, with direct application links, maintained by Simplify and Pitt CSC.
verdict: Yes as a source of postings — but it is a data set, not a workflow. Verify each link before applying; listings go stale.

name: Reactive Resume
description: Privacy-first, self-hostable resume builder: modern templates, import from PDF, role-based sharing links, JSON import/export, PDF/HTML/DOCX export.
verdict: Yes, as the best open resume builder for hosting your own. Better template layer than OpenResume, weaker ATS-analysis layer.

name: Jobs_Applier_AI_Agent (AIHawk)
description: AIHawk: an AI job application bot that narrows millions of postings to the ones matching your resume, then auto-applies by driving a browser. MIT, Python. Widely covered by TechCrunch, Business Insider, Wired and The Verge.
verdict: Yes, but understand the risk profile: mass auto-apply has triggered recruiter scrutiny and platform policy friction. Use it for the search and filtering stage.

name: Resume-Matcher
description: Self-hosted AI harness for building resumes, PDFs and cover letters locally against 100+ LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Gemma), tailoring a CV to a specific job description. Apache-2.0, Next.js + Python.
verdict: Yes. The de-facto reference implementation for tailoring a CV to a JD, and it keeps your documents local.

name: SimplifyJobs/New-Grad-Positions
description: Continuously updated collection of full-time SWE, quant and PM new-grad roles.
verdict: Yes as a postings source for the entry-level search. Same caveat: verify before applying.

name: OpenResume
description: Browser-only resume builder and resume parser: ATS-friendly formatting for Greenhouse and Lever, real-time PDF preview, import from an existing PDF, and a client-side parser to test ATS readability. AGPL-3.0.
verdict: Yes for ATS parsing specifically — its parser is the reason to use it. Runs fully in-browser, nothing leaves the machine. Last push was 2024-10-29, so treat it as stable-but-static.

name: JobSpy
description: Jobs scraper library for LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor, ZipRecruiter, Bayt, Naukri, BDJobs and HelloWork; returns pandas/CSV dataframes and can filter by date, radius, proxy and country.
verdict: Yes, as the data layer under a job agent. Pair it with career-ops rather than running an auto-applier directly against the scraped results.

name: ats-buddy
description: Private-by-design ATS resume analyzer that runs entirely on your machine via WebLLM in the browser or a local Ollama model: match score against a JD, missing technical and soft keywords, actionable suggestions, tailored cover letter and rewritten resume, scanned PDFs read locally. MIT.
verdict: Yes — the only ATS analyzer I verified with no server and no upload. Small project (140 stars) but the privacy property is the point.

name: Jobscan
description: Paid ATS resume scanner: compares your resume against a job description, counts keyword matches against the employer's ATS, flags formatting issues, and provides a 'compare with the job posting' score.
verdict: Skip it if you run ats-buddy or Resume-Matcher locally; the matching logic is the same and the price is not.

name: Simplify.jobs
description: AI job-search platform (free registration plus a Simplify+ subscription): proactive role matching, resume tailoring, browser-form autofill and an Autopilot that auto-applies (claims 50 applications in about 5 minutes of your time). Web and iOS apps; 2M+ job seekers.
verdict: Useful for breadth of listings. Verify each posting on the employer's own ATS - aggregator data ages badly, and Autopilot carries the same policy risk as any auto-applier.

name: Teal
description: AI job search suite (free tier plus a Teal+ paid tier): resume builder, ATS keyword matching against a JD, real-time resume feedback, unlimited job tracking, tailored bullets and cover-letter generation. The free tier requires uploading your resume to their servers.
verdict: Good tracker and keyword UI. The trade-off is that the free tier uploads your resume — ats-buddy gives the same signal with nothing leaving the machine.

name: lmscan
description: Detects AI-generated text and fingerprints which LLM wrote it, offline with zero dependencies: burstiness, sentence-length variance, slop-word density, transition-word ratio, readability consistency. PyPI package, Apache-2.0 license file in-repo.
verdict: Yes, as a pre-publish lint for your own drafts. Treat the score as a smell test, not a verdict — detectors are gameable and Google's policy is about value, not authorship.

name: ai-slop-detector
description: Production-ready AI text classifier built on PyTorch with LoRA, detecting machine-generated content for pre-publication quality gating.
verdict: Only if you have the GPU budget and the training data. The default should be an editorial checklist, not a model.

name: n8n
description: Fair-code workflow automation with native AI capabilities; visual builder plus custom code, 400+ integrations, self-host or cloud.
verdict: Yes, as the glue: schedule crawl → parse → query GSC → post to Slack. The SEO-community n8n nodes (SE Ranking, DataForSEO) extend it.

name: markitdown
description: Converts files and office documents (including PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) into Markdown for LLM consumption.
verdict: Yes — the boring dependency that makes any document pipeline LLM-ready.

name: browser-use
description: Open-source Python library for AI browser agents, plus a cloud with stealth browsers, driving real Chrome through an LLM.
verdict: Yes when a site needs JavaScript or a login. Heavyweight for anything a plain HTTP client can reach.

name: crawl4ai
description: Open-source LLM-friendly web crawler and scraper that emits clean Markdown. The repo powers the hosted Crawl4AI Cloud API (free key, 1,000 credits/month, no card) and can be self-hosted.
verdict: Yes for scraping competitor/AI-answer pages into Markdown for analysis. The hosted API is a fast path; self-host to keep it free.

name: umami
description: Privacy-first web and product analytics: traffic, campaigns, behavior, conversions, no cookie banner; MIT, self-hostable, Docker image.
verdict: Yes, as the analytics of record so you can actually see AI referral traffic (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini) land as sessions and conversions.

name: Plausible Analytics
description: AGPL-3.0, Elixir-based, privacy-first, cookie-free analytics: light and fast, self-hostable, one query per page view.
verdict: Yes as the lightest self-hosted analytics. Less depth than Matomo for AI-referral segmentation.

name: Matomo
description: GPL-3.0 analytics platform with full data ownership, session recording, heatmaps, and — relevant here — a WebAnalytics API and third-party integrations for AI-referral attribution.
verdict: Yes if you need user-level data and cannot use GA4. Heavier to run than Umami.

name: awesome-seo
description: Curated SEO guides, tools and references maintained since 2019, with an explicit policy of refusing vendor and self-promotional listings; expanded recently to cover GEO and agent discoverability.
verdict: Yes, as a reading list with editorial standards. The no-vendor-listing policy makes it more trustworthy than most awesome lists.

name: awesome-generative-engine-optimization
description: Curated GEO resource list covering guides, case studies, tools, research papers, technical documentation, agentic commerce, monitoring and analytics.
verdict: Yes as a map of the field. No license file and it has not been pushed since 2026-04 — treat it as a snapshot, not a live index.

name: awesome-geo
description: Extensive GEO list with research papers (including the Princeton GEO paper), tools and platforms, AI search engines, strategies, analytics and monitoring, plus a GEO checklist. CC0-1.0, English and Chinese.
verdict: Yes — the most current and comprehensive GEO reading list I verified.

name: AutoGEO
description: ICLR 2026 research framework (arXiv 2510.11438) that automatically extracts content-preference rules from generative engines and rewrites documents to maximize visibility while preserving accuracy; GEO score (visibility) and GEU score (utility) metrics; checkpoints and datasets on Hugging Face.
verdict: Read the paper, do not deploy the model. Rule extraction is engine- and dataset-specific, so retraining is required the moment you switch engines.
